title: Creating Custom (Code-Based) Agent Evaluators in Microsoft Foundry with Python
partialText:
AGENTIC AI

Build, register, and debug an evaluator using the Foundry SDK. Plus some common runtime errors discussed.

Introduction

Microsoft Foundry has several built-in evaluators for measuring things such as intent resolution, task adherence, groundedness, and tool-call accuracy. These are a very useful starting point to evaluate an agent because we can add them to an evaluation run without writing the scoring logic ourselves. The setup is also super simple, with the option to create them on Foundry Playground or via SDK.

But what happens when the quality check is specific to our application or agent? Or the agent caters to judgment tasks, like how well did it respond to a customer complaint?

For instance, I have a fact-checker agent that searches the web and returns the sources used to verify a claim. In addition to checking whether the agent understood the task (i.e. intent_resolution), I want to ask a more application-specific question:

Did the agent return enough sources for the input claim and were these sources recent enough?

As of date, there is no built-in evaluator called source_recency, so I created a custom code-based evaluator for it.

The scoring logic (between 0 and 1) is straightforward:

  • 0 if returned sources were not dated (i.e., no published or updated date available)
  • 0.5 if at least one of the returned sources was dated and fulfilled recency requirements
  • 1 if all the returned sources were dated and fulfilled recency requirements

In the rest of the article, we will learn how to (a) write this custom evaluator, (b) register it in Foundry so anyone on your team can call it as easily as the built-in evaluators, and (c) run an eval dataset against it.

Let’s begin!

What are custom code-based evaluators?

A code-based evaluator is a deterministic Python function that Foundry runs for every item in the evaluation dataset. It is useful when the scoring rule can be expressed without asking another LLM to judge the response.

Some examples include:

  • checking whether a response is valid JSON;
  • verifying that mandatory fields are present;
  • measuring response length;
  • detecting whether citations were returned;
  • confirming that enough sources meet a date threshold; or
  • validating an application-specific output format.
Apart from code-based evaluators, we can also create prompt-based evaluators.

Every code-based evaluator must expose a grade function with this shape:

def grade(sample: dict, item: dict) -> float:
    ...

It takes only two inputs — sample which is the output from the agent and item which is each row in the eval dataset.

The function returns a single float between 0.0 and 1.0, where a higher value is better.

Note: Code-based evaluators are best suited to deterministic rules. If the requirement is subjective — for example, “Does this response sound empathetic?” — a prompt-based evaluator is usually a better fit.
Easiest mental mapping is, if you need to use LLM-as-a-judge i.e. an LLM will score an agent output for qualities like politeness, rudeness, sentiment, etc. then use prompt-based evaluator.

Prerequisites

For this example, I am using:

  • Python 3.10 or above;
  • azure-ai-projects==2.8.0;
  • azure-identity;
  • python-dotenv; and
  • an existing Microsoft Foundry project containing an agent and a model deployment.

Install the packages:

pip install azure-ai-projects==2.8.0
pip install azure-identity
pip install python-dotenv

Create a .env file containing the project endpoint and the deployment used by the evaluation service:

AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT="https://<account>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>"
JUDGE_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT="gpt-4o-mini"
Note: The evaluator catalog and some evaluation APIs are still preview features. The exact API surface can change between SDK versions, so pinning the version is helpful when you want the same code to behave consistently across environments.

Our example: a source-recency evaluator

Let’s look at the base agent first

Assume that the fact-checker agent returns JSON containing its final verdict and a list of sources:

{
  "verdict": "True",
  "reasoning": "The claim is supported by recent sources.",
  "sources": [
    {
      "url": "https://example.com/source-a",
      "published_or_updated_date": "2026-10-01"
    },
    {
      "url": "https://example.com/source-b",
      "published_or_updated_date": "2026-09-15"
    }
  ]
}
If you are wondering — do i need to have an agent which returns a JSON object instead of free text?
The answer is — not really! However, it makes life a lot easier if you have a JSON object initialized at the time of agent creation, since we can easily extract entities of interest from it — in this case published_or_updated_date. If it was free text i.e. a string response from the agent, I would need to write complex regex patterns to extract these entities.

Let’s build the eval dataset

Each dataset row (henceforth called an item) carries the policy against which the sources should be checked:

{
  "item": {
    "query": "Claim: Trump administration has launched sustainability campaigns.",
    "as_of_date": "2026-10-09", # today's date
    "max_source_age_days": 180,
    "requires_dated_sources": true,
    "min_sources": 2 # minimum sources needed to verify this claim
  }
}

This is useful because recency is not necessarily a single global rule. One test case might allow sources from the previous 180 days, while another could require information from the last 30 days.

Here’s what the final eval dataset looks like:

{"id": "fc_01", "min_sources": 2, "requires_dated_sources": true, "max_source_age_days": 60, "as_of_date": "2026-10-07", "query": "Claim: Trump administration has launched sustainability campaigns.", "expected_tool_calls": "1 web search (1 claim)", "tool_definitions": [{"name": "web_search", "description": "Searches the web for information to verify a factual claim.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "The search query used to verify a single claim."}}, "required": ["query"]}}]}
{"id": "fc_02", "min_sources": 1, "requires_dated_sources": true, "max_source_age_days": 180, "as_of_date": "2026-10-07", "query": "Claim: Remote work has reduced employee productivity in large technology companies..", "expected_tool_calls": "1 web search (1 claim)", "tool_definitions": [{"name": "web_search", "description": "Searches the web for information to verify a factual claim.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "The search query used to verify a single claim."}}, "required": ["query"]}}]}
{"id": "fc_03", "min_sources": 3, "requires_dated_sources": true, "max_source_age_days": 30, "as_of_date": "2026-10-07", "query": "Claim: Electric vehicles are becoming more environmentally sustainable than petrol cars over their full lifecycle.", "expected_tool_calls": "1 web search (1 claim)", "tool_definitions": [{"name": "web_search", "description": "Searches the web for information to verify a factual claim.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "The search query used to verify a single claim."}}, "required": ["query"]}}]}
{"id": "fc_04", "min_sources": 0, "requires_dated_sources": false, "max_source_age_days": 180, "as_of_date": "2026-10-07", "query": "Claim: Social media platforms have become more effective at limiting the spread of misinformation since 2020.", "expected_tool_calls": "1 web search (1 claim)", "tool_definitions": [{"name": "web_search", "description": "Searches the web for information to verify a factual claim.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "The search query used to verify a single claim."}}, "required": ["query"]}}]}

Writing the grade() function

Here’s the shortened version with helper functions skipped.

def grade(sample: dict, item: dict) -> float:
    """
    Score whether the agent returned enough recent, dated sources.
    """
    try:
        generated_sample = item.get("sample", {})
        response_text = generated_sample.get("output_text", "")

        payload = json.loads(response_text)
        sources = payload.get("sources", [])

        as_of_date = parse_date(item.get("as_of_date"))
        max_age = int(item.get("max_source_age_days", 14))
        min_sources = int(item.get("min_sources", 1))
        requires_dates = bool(item.get("requires_dated_sources", True))

        if not as_of_date or not isinstance(sources, list) or not sources:
            return 0.0

        dated_sources = 0
        recent_sources = 0

        for source in sources:
            source_date = parse_date(
                source.get("published_or_updated_date")
                or source.get("published_date")
                or source.get("updated_date")
            )

            if not source_date:
                continue

            dated_sources += 1
            age_days = (as_of_date - source_date).days

            if 0 <= age_days <= max_age:
                recent_sources += 1

        if recent_sources >= min_sources:
            return 1.0

        if requires_dates and dated_sources == 0:
            return 0.0

        return 0.5 if dated_sources else 0.0

    except Exception:
        return 0.0

A couple of pointers:

  • As explained before, the grade()function expects item dictionary, which in our case looks like this (I will explain shortly how to create this in evals.runs.create()).
item["sample"]["output_text"]
item["as_of_date"]
item["max_source_age_days"]
item["min_sources"]
item["requires_dated_sources"]
  • The agent response (henceforth called sample) should include JSON like:
{
        "sources": [
          {
            "url": "...",
            "published_or_updated_date": "2026-10-01"
          }
        ]
}
  • If you notice line 1 in grade(), we have generated_sample = item.get(“sample”, {}), instead of just generated_sample = sample. This confused me initially — after all, why aren’t we using the sample parameter passed to the grade() directly, instead of calling from inside item?
    Simple answer — This is just the way Msft wants us to do it for the time being; it may change in future API updates. And yes, the grade function must still accept both sample and item, even though the current Foundry target-evaluation path places the generated response inside item.
  • Our fact-checker agent returned a JSON object, but output_text contains its serialized JSON string. We therefore call json.loads() in line 3 before reading sources.

Where did item["sample"]["output_text"] come from?

This was the part I initially found confusing.

I did not add a field called sample to every JSONL row. Foundry adds it at runtime for a model or agent target evaluation. The generated response is currently available to code-based evaluators using:

item.get("sample", {}).get("output_text", "")

The key name sample is not an arbitrary variable chosen by us. It is a Foundry-defined runtime key.

In other words, this will not work automatically:

item["blahblah"]["output_text"]
Note: We could certainly create a dataset field called blahblah, but Foundry would not automatically place the generated agent response inside it. The automatic response is exposed under the reserved sample key. Likewise, output_text is also reserved.

Registering the evaluator

At the time of registering an evaluator using evaluators.create_version(), one of the things you need to define is the data_schema. This schema declares fields specifically required by source_recency for the scoring logic, such as today’s date (as_of_date), age limit (max_source_age_days), and mandatory sources (min_sources) etc., along with their types.

"data_schema" = {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "item": {              <------ place all JSONL columns under item
                        "type": "object",
                        "properties": {
                            "sample": {
                                "type": "object",
                                "properties": {
                                    "output_text": {"type": "string"},
                                },
                            },
                            "as_of_date": {"type": "string"},
                            "max_source_age_days": {"type": "integer"},
                            "requires_dated_sources": {"type": "boolean"},
                            "min_sources": {"type": "integer"},
                        },
                    },
                },
          }

Note: Declaring these fields in data_schema only documents their shape—it does not name or create them. In short, you cannot rename output_text to blahblah and expect Foundry to populate it.

If you will notice, source_recency does not declare query in data_schema because its scoring logic does not use it. However, if the evaluator actually depended on it, you should explicitly add "query": {"type": "string"}.
"data_schema" = {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "item": {
                        "type": "object",
                        "properties": {
                            "sample": {
                                "type": "object",
                                "properties": {
                                    "output_text": {"type": "string"},
                                },
                            },
                            "as_of_date": {"type": "string"},
                            "max_source_age_days": {"type": "integer"},
                            "requires_dated_sources": {"type": "boolean"},
                            "min_sources": {"type": "integer"},
                            "query": {"type": "string"} < -------- newly added
                        },
                    },
                },
          }

Note: The sample argument in grade(sample, item) and the nested item["sample"] can look like the same thing, but they are not interchangeable variables. For the current Foundry target-evaluation contract, Microsoft documents that generated output should be read from the nested value under item.

Creating the evals with the registered evaluator

To make sure the schema for sample is shared with the Foundry evaluators (to allow extracting stuff inside it e.g. sample.output_*), it is important to set include_sample_schema=True when defining the data_source_config

data_source_config = {
    "type": "custom",
    "item_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "query": {"type": "string"},
            "as_of_date": {"type": "string"},
            "max_source_age_days": {"type": "integer"},
            "requires_dated_sources": {"type": "boolean"},
            "min_sources": {"type": "integer"},
        },
        "required": [
            "query",
            "as_of_date",
            "max_source_age_days",
            "requires_dated_sources",
            "min_sources",
        ],
    },
    "include_sample_schema": True, < --- # exposes {{sample.output_*}} and Foundry then supplies them at runtime to code evaluators under item["sample"]
}

This tells the evaluation configuration to expose the generated sample schema. During a target-based evaluation, Foundry constructs the runtime input passed to the evaluator and supplies the generated output under item["sample"].

P.S> It does not rewrite the original JSONL file or permanently append a sample object to the dataset row.

Registering the evaluator

The evaluator code must be registered in the Foundry evaluator catalog before it can be referenced by an evaluation.

The important part of the registration is in the snippet above, using project_client.evaluators.create_version().

evaluator = project_client.evaluators.create_version(
            name = "source_recency",
            headers = ...,
            evaluator_version = {
                "name": "source_recency",
                "categories": [EvaluatorCategory.QUALITY],
                "display_name": "Source Recency",
                "description": "Checks whether returned sources are recent enough for the test case policy.",
                "definition": { 
                     ...,
                    "data_schema": {
                        "type": "object",
                        "properties": {
                            "item": {
                                "type": "object",
                                "properties": {
                                    "sample": {
                                        "type": "object",
                                        "properties": {
                                            "output_text": {"type": "string"},
                                        },
                                    },
                                    "as_of_date": {"type": "string"},
                                    "max_source_age_days": {"type": "integer"},
                                    "requires_dated_sources": {"type": "boolean"},
                                    "min_sources": {"type": "integer"},
                                },
                            },
                        },
                    },
                  }
            }
)

Run the registration script once:

python register_evaluator.py

You should see the newly created version printed in the terminal.

Note: “Run once” means once per evaluator version — not once for the evaluator’s entire lifetime. Do not register it before every evaluation run. Run the script again only when the evaluator code or definition changes, because create_version() creates another catalog version.

Pin the evaluator version

After creating a new version, pass that version in the testing criterion:

SOURCE_RECENCY_EVALUATOR_VERSION = os.getenv(
    "SOURCE_RECENCY_EVALUATOR_VERSION"
)

source_recency_criterion = {
    "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
    "name": "source_recency",
    "evaluator_name": "source_recency",
    "evaluator_version": SOURCE_RECENCY_EVALUATOR_VERSION,
    "initialization_parameters": {
        "deployment_name": JUDGE_MODEL,
        "pass_threshold": 0.2,
    },
}
You may ask — Why pin it when the SDK says it can use the latest version?
During development, I had several versions of the same evaluator registered with different schemas. One version expected the flat fields response, as_of_date, and min_sources, while a later version expected only item. An evaluation resolved the older contract and failed with MissingRequiredDataMapping.

P.S. You need one criterion dictionary per evaluator. So if you are using source_recency along with the inbuilt task_adherence evaluator, you will have:

source_recency_criterion = {
    "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
    "name": "source_recency",
    "evaluator_name": "source_recency",
    "evaluator_version": SOURCE_RECENCY_EVALUATOR_VERSION,
    "initialization_parameters": {
        "deployment_name": JUDGE_MODEL,
        "pass_threshold": 0.2,
    },
}

task_adherence_criterion = {
    "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
    "name": "task_adherence",
    "evaluator_name": "builtin.task_adherence",
    "evaluator_version": SOURCE_RECENCY_EVALUATOR_VERSION,
    "initialization_parameters": {
        "model": JUDGE_MODEL,
    },
    "data_mapping": {
        "query": "{{item.query}}",
        "response": "{{sample.output_items}}"
    }
}

criteria = [source_recency_criterion, task_adherence_criterion]

This will be used for creating evals later on:

item_properties = {
            "query": {"type": "string"},
            "as_of_date": {"type": "string"},
            "max_source_age_days": {"type": "integer"},
            "requires_dated_sources": {"type": "boolean"},
            "min_sources": {"type": "integer"},
        }

required = [
            "query",
            "as_of_date",
            "max_source_age_days",
            "requires_dated_sources",
            "min_sources",
        ]

eval_object = openai_client.evals.create(
        name=f"{agent_key} dataset evaluation",
        data_source_config={
            "type": "custom",
            "item_schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": item_properties,
                "required": required,
            },
            "include_sample_schema": True,   # exposes {{sample.output_*}} and Foundry then supplies them at runtime to code evaluators under item["sample"]
        },
        testing_criteria=criteria,
    )

A couple of things:

  • Criterion will look different depending on the evaluator you are using. For example, observe how we don’t need to pass on data_mapping parameter for custom evaluators like source_recency. This is because, unlike the built-in evaluators, a Foundry code-based evaluator does not need an explicit data_mapping. Its registered data_schema requires item, and its dataset fields are read from that dictionary.

Built-in evaluators need data mappings; this code evaluator does not

Built-in evaluators describe the inputs they expect. For example, an intent-resolution evaluator needs a query and a response:

{
    "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
    "name": "intent_resolution",
    "evaluator_name": "builtin.intent_resolution",
    "initialization_parameters": {"model": JUDGE_MODEL},
    "data_mapping": {
        "query": "{{item.query}}",
        "response": "{{sample.output_text}}",
    },
}

So we use data_mapping dictionary where key is what an evaluator might need for evaluation, and the value is the location where to find it. For instance, the query for intent-resolution comes from the eval dataset, i.e. item and can be found at item.query. Likewise, intent-resolution also needs the response to check whether intent was resolved in the final agent output. To do this, it can use sample.output_text.

Other evaluators like tool_call_accuracy might instead need the structured response items

"data_mapping": {
        "query": "{{item.query}}",
        "response": "{{sample.output_items}}",
    },

So why don’t we need a data_mapping for a custom evaluator?

Unlike the built-in evaluators, a Foundry code-based evaluator does not need an explicit data_mapping.

The code-based source_recency evaluator is different. Its registered schema requires the complete item object, and Foundry supplies the generated target sample inside that object. Therefore, its testing criterion does not need an explicit data_mapping.

P.S. This is not a general rule that all custom evaluator types ignore mappings. It is the contract used by Foundry code-based evaluators. Prompt-based and endpoint-based evaluators have their own input and mapping requirements.

Since I was not aware of this initially, I made the mistake of adding explicit mappings to the code evaluator. My scoring logic, i.e. grade() needed sample and item and this is how I created the data mapping:

"data_mapping": {
    "sample": "{{sample.output_text}}",
    "item": "{{item.recency_input}}",
}

Funnily enough, the evaluation run completed without errors, but the fact-checker agent responded as if the user had literally asked it to score intent-resolution for this input query: {{item.query}}

The built-in evaluators also produced strange results, which initially made it look as though all the evaluators were broken. But the evaluators were downstream of the same generated response. The real issue was that the agent target had received an unresolved input template. Also, looking at intent_resolution.reason column confirmed my doubts that the actual user input was never passed.

To debug, I tried removing source_recency and that made the built-in evaluations work again. That was the useful clue: the problem was not the dataset query or the built-in evaluators; it was the custom criterion’s contract, i.e. data_mapping.

The fix was to follow the code-based evaluator pattern:

  • declare item in the registered data_schema;
  • enable the sample schema for the target evaluation;
  • read the generated response from item["sample"]["output_text"]; and
  • omit data_mapping from the code-evaluator criterion.
Pro Tip: When adding a new evaluator breaks an otherwise working target run, temporarily remove only that evaluator. If the agent starts receiving the correct query again, compare the custom evaluator’s registered schema with its testing criterion before changing the agent prompt or dataset.
criteria = [
    # source_recency_criterion,  <--- temporarily remove custom evaluator
    task_adherence_criterion
]

eval_object = openai_client.evals.create(
        name=f"{agent_key} dataset evaluation",
        data_source_config=data_source_config,
        testing_criteria=criteria
    )

Why is there no source_recency.reason column?

If you look at Figure 2 above, you’ll notice all built-in evaluators often show both a score and a reason in the Foundry report. For instance,

intent_resolution
intent_resolution.reason

A code-based evaluator has a smaller output contract: grade() returns a single float. Consequently, our report contains source_recency, but it does not contain source_recency.reason.

This is expected behaviour — not a missing schema field.

If an explanation is mandatory, there are two alternatives:

  1. Use a prompt-based evaluator, which can return result and reason.
  2. Use an endpoint-based evaluator, which can return score, reason, statusand optional properties.

I kept source-recency code-based because its scoring rule is deterministic and does not need another LLM call. For this scenario, predictable scoring was more important than generating a natural-language reason for every row.

Complete evaluation workflow

At a high level, the final flow looks like this:

  1. Load each JSONL row into item.
  2. Foundry renders {{item.query}} and sends it to the agent target.
  3. The agent generates its fact-checking response.
  4. Because the sample schema is enabled, Foundry makes that generated response available to the code evaluator under item["sample"].
  5. grade(sample, item) parses item["sample"]["output_text"].
  6. The evaluator checks the source dates against the policy fields from the same item.
  7. Foundry records the returned float as the source_recency score.

The key evaluation configuration is:

eval_object = openai_client.evals.create(
    name="fact-checker dataset evaluation",
    data_source_config={
        "type": "custom",
        "item_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": item_properties,
            "required": required,
        },
        "include_sample_schema": True,
    },
    testing_criteria=testing_criteria,
)

The target run then connects each dataset query to the agent:

run = openai_client.evals.runs.create(
    eval_id=eval_object.id,
    name="fact-checker dataset run",
    data_source={
        "type": "azure_ai_target_completions",
        "source": {
            "type": "file_content",
            "content": rows,
        },
        "input_messages": {
            "type": "template",
            "template": [
                {
                    "type": "message",
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": {
                        "type": "input_text",
                        "text": "{{item.query}}",
                    },
                }
            ],
        },
        "target": {
            "type": "azure_ai_agent",
            "name": "fact-checker-agent",
        },
    },
)

A couple of pointers:

  • Setting “type”: “azure_ai_target_completions” is to let Foundry know we don't have ground truth responses, so each query in the eval dataset must be run against the fact-checker agent, and generated responses will be used for the evaluations.
  • Under input_messages the role user is used for passing in the query (if you have worked with the openai or langchain library, this way of sending payload should look familiar).
  • When you are creating the content each row must contain everything that will be needed by the evaluator for the scoring. For instance, at a basic level:
item1 = {
          "query": "Ice caps are melting fast"
          "as_of_date": "26 Oct 2026"
          "max_source_age_days": 180
          "requires_dated_sources": True
          "min_sources": 2,
}

rows = [{"item": item1}, {"item": item2}, .....]
content = rows

Interestingly, you can also send additional context in each dataset item for built-in evaluators. For example, if I were using the built-in task-adherence evaluator to evaluate a risk-assessment agent, it makes sense to pass in my company-specific guidelines to tell the evaluator what constitutes a high vs medium vs low risk rather than letting the evaluator use its own inherent judgment.

COMPANY_SYSTEM_PROMPT = "If they experience rashes, make as high risk, ...."

{
    "query": "I used your medicines and experiened rashes."
    "task_adherence_query": [
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": COMPANY_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "I used your medicines and experiened rashes.",
        },
    ],
}

And later on, to make sure it is used, I will update the data_mapping

"data_mapping": 
    {
        "query": "{{item.task_adherence_query}}",
        "response": "{{sample.output_items}}",
    }

So there are two distinct inputs:

  • input_messages calls the agent. (The agent already receives its system instructions from its registered definition, so no need to pass the system prompt again).
  • task_adherence_query gives the evaluator both the system prompt and user query.

Final Thoughts

Creating the scoring function was the easy part. The more valuable lesson was understanding the boundary between the dataset item, the target-generated sample, and the evaluator’s registered schema.

The main points I would remember are:

  • code-based evaluators always expose grade(sample, item);
  • for a Foundry model or agent target, generated text is currently available under item["sample"]["output_text"];
  • sample is a reserved runtime key—it cannot be renamed to blahblah and still receive the generated response automatically;
  • built-in evaluators commonly need explicit mappings, while this code-based evaluator does not;
  • registration creates versions, so pin the version used by the evaluation; and
  • code-based evaluators return a score only, without a .reason column.

Once these contracts are clear, custom code-based evaluators become a powerful way to turn application-specific expectations into repeatable quality checks.

Happy Learning 🚀

Creating Custom (Code-Based) Agent Evaluators in Microsoft Foundry with Python was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: How to Ship Safely With Feature Flags: OpenFeature, Gradual Rollouts and Kill Switches
partialText:
A Hands-On TypeScript Guide to Decoupling Deploys From Releases, With Tested Code for Targeting, Telemetry and Flag Cleanup

Most production incidents do not start with a bad idea. They start with a good change that reached every user at the same moment. A new checkout flow, a rewritten search query or a migration to a new payment provider can pass every test and still fail under real traffic, and when it does, the only lever many teams have is a rollback that takes 20 minutes and another deploy. Feature flags fix that by separating two things we usually treat as one: deploying code and releasing behaviour.

The catch is that flags are easy to add and hard to live with. Every flag is a branch in production that nobody tests in every combination, a hidden configuration dependency and, if it is never removed, a piece of permanent debt. Teams also tend to lock themselves into one vendor SDK that ends up sprinkled through hundreds of files. In this post we will build a small but realistic setup in TypeScript with OpenFeature, the vendor-neutral flag API, and flagd as the flag engine: percentage rollouts, user targeting, a kill switch, evaluation telemetry and an automated check that stops flags from living forever. Every code sample was run against @openfeature/server-sdk 1.23.0 and @openfeature/flagd-provider 0.18.0.

The Problem

Without flags, a release is binary. The moment a deploy finishes, 100% of users get the new code. If something goes wrong, you roll back the whole deploy, including any unrelated fixes that shipped with it. That pushes teams towards long-lived branches, big releases and release-day nerves.

The opposite failure is just as real. The most famous feature flag accident is the Knight Capital incident of August 1, 2012. According to the SEC order, Knight reused an old flag to switch on new trading code, but one of its eight servers never received the new deploy. On that server the flag woke up dormant code from years earlier, which sent more than 4 million executions into the market in about 45 minutes and cost the firm over $460 million. The lessons are still relevant: never repurpose a flag, remove dead code behind old flags, and make sure every instance evaluates flags the same way.

So we want three things at once: the ability to release gradually and turn things off instantly, a consistent evaluation model across services, and a process that keeps the number of flags under control.

Core Concepts

Pete Hodgson’s classic article on martinfowler.com sorts flags into four categories by how long they live and how dynamic they are. Knowing which kind you are creating decides how you should manage it:

  • Release toggles hide unfinished or risky code while it rolls out. They should live days or weeks, then be deleted.
  • Experiment toggles split users into cohorts for A/B tests and must stay stable long enough to give meaningful results.
  • Ops toggles let operators degrade or disable a feature during an incident. Most are short-lived, but a few kill switches stay forever.
  • Permission toggles expose features to certain users, such as internal staff or paying customers, and can last for years.

On the tooling side, OpenFeature is a CNCF project that standardises the API your code calls, while a provider plugs in the actual flag system. It became a CNCF incubating project in December 2023. The key terms:

  • Provider: the adapter to a flag backend. We will use flagd, the open source flag engine from the OpenFeature project, but the same code works with commercial vendors that ship providers.
  • Client: the object your code uses to evaluate flags, optionally scoped to a domain such as “checkout”.
  • Evaluation context: the attributes a rule can use, such as user ID, plan or region. The targetingKey is the stable identifier used for percentage rollouts.
  • Hooks: code that runs before, after or on error of every evaluation, ideal for logging and metrics.
  • Resolution details: besides the value, every evaluation can return the variant, a reason such as TARGETING_MATCH or ERROR, and an error code.

Step 1: Install the SDK and Choose a Provider Mode

npm install @openfeature/server-sdk @openfeature/flagd-provider

The flagd provider supports two resolver types. In rpc mode, the default, each evaluation is a call to a flagd daemon on port 8013. In in-process mode, the provider downloads the flag definitions and evaluates them inside your Node.js process, so there is no network hop per flag. For this tutorial we use in-process mode with a local file through offlineFlagSourcePath, which is also handy in tests. In production you would point the same provider at a flagd instance or sync source instead.

Step 2: Define Flags as Code

flagd flags are JSON documents with variants, a default variant and optional targeting rules written in JSONLogic. Here are two flags: a release toggle for a new checkout flow and a long-lived kill switch for search.

{
  "$schema": "https://flagd.dev/schema/v0/flags.json",
  "flags": {
    "new-checkout": {
      "state": "ENABLED",
      "variants": { "on": true, "off": false },
      "defaultVariant": "off",
      "metadata": { "owner": "team-payments", "expires": "2026-12-15" },
      "targeting": {
        "if": [
          { "in": [{ "var": "email" }, ["qa@example.com"]] }, "on",
          { "==": [{ "var": "plan" }, "internal"] }, "on",
          { "fractional": [["on", 10], ["off", 90]] }
        ]
      }
    },
    "search-kill-switch": {
      "state": "ENABLED",
      "variants": { "enabled": true, "disabled": false },
      "defaultVariant": "enabled",
      "metadata": { "owner": "team-search", "expires": "never" }
    }
  }
}

The targeting rule for new-checkout reads from top to bottom: the QA account always gets the new flow, internal staff always get it, and everyone else goes through a 10/90 split. The fractional operation hashes the flag key together with the targeting key using murmur3, so the same user always lands in the same bucket, and different flags bucket users independently. To move from 10% to 25%, you change the weights. Users already in the "on" bucket stay there as the percentage grows, which avoids people flipping back and forth between experiences.

Notice the metadata block. flagd passes it through to your application, and we will use the owner and expiry fields in Step 6 to keep flags from becoming permanent.

Step 3: Evaluate Flags With Request Context

The cleanest way to use flags in a web service is to set the evaluation context once per request and let every evaluation pick it up automatically. The server SDK supports this through a transaction context propagator built on Node.js AsyncLocalStorage. Here is a small Express service:

import express from 'express';
import { OpenFeature, AsyncLocalStorageTransactionContextPropagator, ProviderEvents } from '@openfeature/server-sdk';
import { FlagdProvider } from '@openfeature/flagd-provider';
import { FlagTelemetryHook } from './telemetry-hook.mts';
OpenFeature.setTransactionContextPropagator(new AsyncLocalStorageTransactionContextPropagator());
OpenFeature.addHooks(new FlagTelemetryHook());
OpenFeature.addHandler(ProviderEvents.Error, (e) => console.error('flag provider error', e?.message));
try {
  await OpenFeature.setProviderAndWait(new FlagdProvider({ resolverType: 'in-process', offlineFlagSourcePath: './flags.json' }));
} catch (err) {
  console.error('flags unavailable, serving defaults', err);
}
const flags = OpenFeature.getClient('checkout');
const app = express();
app.use((req, _res, next) => {
  const userId = req.header('x-user-id') ?? 'anonymous';
  OpenFeature.setTransactionContext(
    { targetingKey: userId, plan: req.header('x-plan') ?? 'free', email: req.header('x-email') ?? '' },
    () => next(),
  );
});
app.get('/checkout', async (_req, res) => {
  const useNewCheckout = await flags.getBooleanValue('new-checkout', false);
  res.json({ flow: useNewCheckout ? 'v2' : 'v1' });
});
app.get('/search', async (_req, res) => {
  const searchOn = await flags.getBooleanValue('search-kill-switch', true);
  if (!searchOn) return res.status(503).json({ message: 'Search is temporarily unavailable' });
  res.json({ results: [] });
});
const server = app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'));
process.on('SIGTERM', async () => { server.close(); await OpenFeature.close(); });

A few details matter here:

  • The middleware sets context once. Any code that runs inside that request, however deep in the call stack, evaluates flags against the same user without passing the user around.
  • Every evaluation has a safe default. If the flag is missing, the provider fails or the value has the wrong type, getBooleanValue returns the default instead of throwing. For a release toggle the safe default is the old behaviour (false). For a kill switch it is "feature on" (true), so a broken flag system does not take search down with it.
  • Startup does not depend on flags. If the provider cannot initialise, the service logs it and keeps serving defaults rather than crashing.
  • Shutdown is clean. OpenFeature.close() releases provider connections and file watchers.

Before trusting a rollout, check that the split behaves as you expect. This script evaluates the flag for 10,000 synthetic users and prints the details of one targeted evaluation:

import { OpenFeature } from '@openfeature/server-sdk';
import { FlagdProvider } from '@openfeature/flagd-provider';
await OpenFeature.setProviderAndWait(new FlagdProvider({ resolverType: 'in-process', offlineFlagSourcePath: './flags.json' }));
const flags = OpenFeature.getClient('rollout-check');
let enabled = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
  const ctx = { targetingKey: `user-${i}`, plan: 'free' };
  if (await flags.getBooleanValue('new-checkout', false, ctx)) enabled++;
}
console.log(`new-checkout enabled for ${enabled / 100}% of users`);
const details = await flags.getBooleanDetails('new-checkout', false, { targetingKey: 'qa-1', email: 'qa@example.com' });
console.log(details.value, details.variant, details.reason, details.flagMetadata);
await OpenFeature.close();
new-checkout enabled for 9.85% of users
true on TARGETING_MATCH { owner: 'team-payments', expires: '2026-12-15' }

9.85% is as close to 10% as a hash-based split should be, and the details object tells us exactly why the QA user got the new flow.

Step 4: Add Telemetry With Hooks

A flag you cannot observe is a flag you cannot safely change. When error rates move during a rollout, the first question is “which variant were the failing requests on?” Hooks answer it. This hook logs every evaluation and every error as structured JSON:

import type { Hook, HookContext, EvaluationDetails, FlagValue } from '@openfeature/server-sdk';
export class FlagTelemetryHook implements Hook {
  after(ctx: HookContext, details: EvaluationDetails<FlagValue>) {
    console.log(JSON.stringify({
      event: 'flag_evaluated', flag: ctx.flagKey, variant: details.variant,
      reason: details.reason, user: ctx.context.targetingKey,
    }));
  }
  error(ctx: HookContext, err: unknown) {
    console.warn(JSON.stringify({ event: 'flag_error', flag: ctx.flagKey, message: (err as Error).message }));
  }
}

Calling the service with a QA user, an internal user and an anonymous search request produced these lines:

{"event":"flag_evaluated","flag":"new-checkout","variant":"on","reason":"TARGETING_MATCH","user":"u1"}
{"event":"flag_evaluated","flag":"new-checkout","variant":"on","reason":"TARGETING_MATCH","user":"u2"}
{"event":"flag_evaluated","flag":"search-kill-switch","variant":"enabled","reason":"STATIC","user":"anonymous"}

In a real system you would not log every evaluation at info level on a busy endpoint. Sample it, or attach the flag and variant to your traces instead. The OpenFeature project publishes @openfeature/open-telemetry-hooks for exactly that, and if you already trace your services, the approach in my post on tracing LLM apps with OpenTelemetry applies here too: put the flag variant on the span, then compare latency and error rate per variant on one dashboard.

Step 5: Use the Kill Switch in an Incident

The search kill switch is an ops toggle. During an incident, for example a search cluster that is timing out and dragging down the whole API, an operator changes one value:

"defaultVariant": "disabled"

With the in-process provider watching the file, the running service picked up the change within a few seconds without a restart, and the next request returned a clean 503 with a friendly message instead of a timeout. In production the change would go through your flag backend or a reviewed pull request to the flag repository, but the effect is the same: you degrade one feature in seconds instead of rolling back a deploy in minutes. Practise this before you need it. A kill switch that has never been flipped is a theory, not a safety net.

Step 6: Stop Flag Debt in CI

Hodgson suggests treating flags as inventory with a carrying cost, with expiry dates and even “time bombs” that fail tests when a flag outlives its date. Because our flags are code with metadata, that is a short script we can run in CI:

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
type FlagMeta = { owner?: string; expires?: string };
const { flags } = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./flags.json', 'utf8')) as {
  flags: Record<string, { metadata?: FlagMeta }>;
};
const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
const problems: string[] = [];
for (const [key, { metadata }] of Object.entries(flags)) {
  if (!metadata?.owner || !metadata?.expires) {
    problems.push(`${key}: missing owner or expires`);
  } else if (metadata.expires !== 'never' && metadata.expires < today) {
    problems.push(`${key}: expired on ${metadata.expires}, owner ${metadata.owner}`);
  }
}
if (problems.length > 0) {
  console.error(`Flag hygiene check failed:\n${problems.join('\n')}`);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log(`All ${Object.keys(flags).length} flags have an owner and a valid expiry`);

When I moved the expiry of new-checkout into the past, the check failed with a clear message and a non-zero exit code:

Flag hygiene check failed:
new-checkout: expired on 2026-10-01, owner team-payments

Now every flag needs an owner and an end date before it can be merged, permanent flags must say so explicitly with "never", and an expired release toggle blocks the pipeline until someone either removes it or consciously extends it. That is the conversation you want to force.

Common Pitfalls

  • Reusing a flag name for a new purpose. This is the Knight Capital mistake. Old code paths and old configuration can still react to the name. Always create a new flag and delete the old one completely.
  • Using an unstable targeting key. If you bucket by session ID, users switch variants when they log in on another device. Use a stable user or account ID, and for B2B products consider bucketing by organisation so a whole team sees the same behaviour.
  • Changing the bucketing expression mid-rollout. The flagd docs warn that renaming a flag, reordering variants or switching between the default and a custom bucketing expression reassigns users. Pick the scheme before you start.
  • Unsafe defaults. A default that enables an untested path is a time bomb the day your flag backend is unreachable. Defaults should always mean “the behaviour we already trust”.
  • Evaluating flags in hot loops. In RPC mode every evaluation is a network call. Evaluate once per request and pass the result down, or use in-process mode.
  • Testing only the “on” path. At minimum, test the current production configuration, the intended release configuration and the fallback configuration.
  • Putting secrets or personal data in context. Evaluation context ends up in logs and hooks. Send only what rules need, and avoid raw email addresses where an internal ID will do.

Best Practices

  1. Name flags for what they do and keep one purpose per flag. new-checkout and search-kill-switch tell an on-call engineer at 3 a.m. what will happen when they change them.
  2. Roll out in stages with exit criteria. Internal users, then 1%, 10%, 50% and 100%, with agreed error rate and latency thresholds between steps, written down before you start.
  3. Keep flag definitions in version control. Pull requests give you review, history and an easy revert for flag changes, the same way they do for code.
  4. Hide the vendor behind OpenFeature. Your application code only depends on the standard API, so moving from flagd to a commercial service, or the other way round, is a provider change rather than a rewrite.
  5. Make flags observable. Every evaluation should be traceable to a variant, so dashboards can compare old and new behaviour side by side.
  6. Delete release toggles as part of done. A feature is not finished when it reaches 100%. It is finished when the flag and the old code path are gone.

Final Thoughts

Feature flags turn releases from a single risky moment into a controlled process: ship the code dark, expose it to a few users, watch the numbers, and keep a switch within reach. OpenFeature makes that process portable, flagd gives you a capable open source engine to start with, and a few lines of hooks and CI checks keep flags observable and short-lived. The hard part is not the code. It is the discipline to set safe defaults, measure every rollout and delete flags when they have done their job.

How does your team manage feature flags today, and have you ever been bitten by one that lived too long? Share your story in the comments.

Sources: OpenFeature Docs, flagd Docs, npm: flagd provider, martinfowler.com, SEC, CNCF

title: I told Claude to hold off on isolation. Its networks took two of our LAN’s subnets.
partialText:
At 14:49 on October 13, I pasted two lines from a production host’s routing table into my Claude Code session:

192.168.16.0    0.0.0.0         255.255.240.0   U         0 0          0 br-f1a328c0938f
192.168.32.0    0.0.0.0         255.255.240.0   U         0 0          0 br-0adbee56597f

Two /20 blocks, each sent to a Docker bridge. Machines on our LAN live in those ranges. From that host, traffic for anything between 192.168.16.0 and 192.168.47.255 went into the bridges instead of the network. I added one sentence, in French: “tu m’as fait un incident en prod”. You gave me a production incident.

The first line of the answer said it was very probably its doing. It was. The part worth telling is what I had said before: I had asked to hold off on isolating that service, and the networks that broke the routes were the isolation.

Some context. I run backend engineering at GoodBarber, an app platform. That morning, with Claude Code, I was putting a new internal service on two of our Docker hosts. Its spec said that one of its containers must eventually reach nothing on our network. I had given Claude the right to deploy through our Buildbot pipeline, and it wrote the deploy files and an isolation test that runs at every deploy.

Where the subnets came from

The compose file declared networks without a fixed range. When a network has no ipam subnet, Docker takes the next free block in its default pools: 172.17.0.0/16 to 172.31.0.0/16 first, then 192.168.0.0/16 cut into /20 blocks. On that host, the 172 ranges were already used, so the new networks landed in 192.168.0.0/16.

Docker skips the blocks it knows are taken. Our hosts reach those two ranges through a router, so nothing on the host said they were in use. Each new bridge came with its own route, and from then on the host sent traffic for those ranges to the bridge.

The networks appeared at 11:35, on the first deploy that got past the secrets step. They stayed until I stopped the service, a little after 14:50. For about three hours, that host’s traffic to two of our LAN’s ranges went nowhere. In practice, our failover took over, and end users saw nothing.

What I had said, and when

I went back through the session to see what Claude had been told. The times are Paris time, and the quotes are my translations.

  • 11:23. The first deploy had failed, and I asked whether we could skip the iptables rule for now and add it just before the official release. Claude postponed the iptables rule. It kept the isolated networks from the spec, and the isolation test, which still failed the deploy if the container could reach the LAN, the Internet or DNS. Only the checks on the host itself became warnings.
  • 11:46. About another part of the setup, I wrote that the LAN is private, that it shouldn’t overthink it, and that it should make something that works on the LAN.
  • 12:09. Claude added a Redis container for the service, on a network of its own. I asked why it wanted one, then accepted it and asked to keep it isolated. That third network is on me.
  • 13:37. I asked to put everything in production. Claude asked one question first, and the option it recommended put the iptables rule back and made the host check blocking. I said not to apply anything in production.
  • 14:49. The two routes.
  • 14:51. “I’m repeating my recommendation: don’t isolate it during the test phase.” Then I asked for a solution that obeyed me and left the routes alone, and said we would leave the isolation to ops.

Read in order, my 11:23 message only named the iptables rule. Claude postponed exactly that and kept everything else the spec asked for. The spec was detailed and had been there since the start of the session. My instruction came later, in one sentence, about one mechanism. When the two disagreed, the spec won, and it went on winning at 13:37, when the recommended option brought back the rule I had postponed.

Claude listened to my words and missed what I meant. It read “skip the iptables for now” as a list of one item, and kept the spec as the goal. What I meant was “no isolation during the test phase”, and I only wrote it in those words after the incident. Claude knew our convention, too. Its apology ended with: “I should have pinned the ranges from the start, or better, followed the convention of your services and stayed on the default bridge.”

The fix

The fix, commit d232579 at 14:54, removed every network from the compose file. The four containers moved to the host's default bridge, like our other services, and find each other by name. The deploy script deletes the three old networks if they still exist, with their routes, since docker-compose down no longer knows about them. The isolation test still runs, but whatever the container can reach is only reported as a warning. The isolation itself is left to ops.

The redeploy failed at 14:56. The isolation test runs from inside the service’s image, and that deploy hadn’t rebuilt it, so the old test still treated the LAN, the Internet and DNS as blocking. A full pipeline, build then deploy, went green at 14:58, with no Creating network line in the logs.

Claude also wrote a rule into its memory for that repository: never create a Docker network on these hosts without a range validated with ops, stay on the default bridge by default, and ask before any Docker network change in production.

What I’d check on your hosts

  • ip route after any deploy that creates a network. A br- route in a range your LAN uses is the incident.
  • Pinned subnets in your compose files, or default-address-pools in daemon.json set to a range you own. We had neither on those hosts. A pool looks like this, with a base your LAN and VPNs don't use:
{
  "default-address-pools": [
    { "base": "10.200.0.0/16", "size": 24 }
  ]
}
  • The compose files your agent writes, for networks: without ipam. A spec that asks for isolation will produce them.

When you change your mind in the middle of a session, where do you write it so that it outweighs the spec your agent started from?

Originally published at https://dev.to on October 30, 2026.

title: My GPU fix was 13% faster on one card and 81% slower on another
partialText:
A vLLM int8 GEMM change, a reviewer with a smaller Ada GPU, and the one idea that explained it: waves

On October 17 I opened a small vLLM pull request that made int8 matrix multiplies about 13% faster on an RTX 4090. The next day a reviewer ran it on a smaller Ada card and one layer got up to 81% slower.

Same code, same kind of GPU, opposite result. This post is about why, and about the rule that fixed it on three different Ada GPUs. The PR is vLLM #62128. It’s open and waiting for a maintainer’s review, so everything here is work in progress, not something that’s in vLLM yet.

The bug report

vLLM issue #56924 reported that int8 W8A8 GEMMs on Ada (SM89) get about 1.5x slower when the number of tokens M goes from 16 to 17, and again from 32 to 33. That’s the batch range a server lives in during decode, so it matters.

The cause was in the dispatch code that picks a CUTLASS tile shape based on M:

For the small layers of a model like Qwen3–1.7B (N = 2048), bigger tiles mean fewer thread blocks. With 64-column tiles, N = 2048 gives 32 tiles across. At M = 17 with 32-row tiles that’s 32 thread blocks in total, on a GPU with 128 SMs. Most of the GPU sits idle, and each block does twice the work.

On my RTX 4090, q_proj jumped from 4.92 µs at M = 16 to 7.81 µs at M = 17.

The first fix

The obvious fix: keep the 16-row tiles past M = 16 for small layers. More, smaller blocks, more of the GPU busy. I used an N limit to decide what “small” meant (N ≤ 4096 for M up to 32, N ≤ 2048 up to 64), measured it on the 4090, and the numbers were good:

  • about 13% less total GEMM time over M = 17–64 across six Qwen3–1.7B shapes (409.5 → 355.3 µs)
  • q_proj at M = 17: 7.81 → 5.53 µs
  • identical results, all 400 int8 tests passing

I opened the PR and wrote in the description that I had only measured it on a 4090.

The review

The next day Shikha Pallavi ran it on an RTX 4500 Ada and posted every number on the PR. qkv_proj got 21% faster. But down_proj got 35–81% slower at every M the change touched, and o_proj at M = 64 got 24% slower.

The RTX 4500 Ada has 60 SMs. The 4090 has 128. That turned out to be the whole story.

Waves

A GPU runs thread blocks on its SMs. If there are more blocks than can run at once, the extra ones wait and run in a second round, a second wave. The kernel isn’t done until the last wave finishes.

For these int8 kernels the tiles use a lot of shared memory (51–80 KB against Ada’s 100 KB per SM), so each SM runs one block at a time. That makes the math simple: waves = ceil(blocks / SMs).

Take down_proj (N = 2048) at M = 17:

On the 4090, 64 smaller blocks all run at once and finish sooner. That’s the 13%. On the 4500 Ada, 60 of them run, then the last 4 run alone while 56 SMs wait. Each block is faster, but you pay for a whole extra round. That’s the slowdown.

Looking back at my own 4090 data, every case where the 16-row tiles had lost was a case where they added a wave. I’d picked an N limit that happened to avoid those on 128 SMs. On 60 SMs it didn’t.

I put the PR back in draft and thanked the reviewer. They were right, and they’d tested it on hardware I didn’t have.

The new rule

Instead of guessing from N, count the waves. The dispatch now reads the SM count once per device and uses the 16-row tiles only when:

  1. they fit in the same number of waves as the stock tiles, or
  2. the stock tiles already need two or more waves, and the 16-row tiles add at most half again as many.
waves_16    = ceil(ceil(M / 16) * n_tiles / SMs)
waves_stock = ceil(ceil(M / stock_rows) * n_tiles / SMs)
use 16-row tiles if  waves_16 == waves_stock
                 or (waves_stock >= 2 and 2 * waves_16 <= 3 * waves_stock)

The second part exists for one case: qkv_proj (N = 4096) on a 60-SM card goes from 2 waves to 3, and it was still faster in the reviewer's run. When the GPU is already doing several rounds, smaller blocks fill the last round better. That 1.5x allowance is the one part of the rule fitted to data, so it needed checking on real hardware.

On the 4090 the new rule picks exactly the same tiles as my first version for all six shapes. On 58–60 SMs it keeps the stock tiles for down_proj and o_proj and keeps the 16-row tiles only for k/v_proj and the small-M qkv_proj.

Checking it on three GPUs

L4 (58 SMs, my own run). I rented an L4, built vLLM from source with the exact file that’s in the commit, and ran the same benchmark for stock, my first version and the new rule:

Every cell the wave rule changes got faster, 0.59–0.82x of stock. Every other cell runs the stock kernel. The int8 tests pass: 400 passed, 54 skipped.

RTX 4500 Ada (60 SMs, the reviewer’s rerun). After I pushed the new commit, the reviewer ran it again on the card that caught the problem: 626.2 → 602.4 µs over the same range (3.8% less, with two repeats at 3.1% and 3.5%). It changed exactly the cells the rule predicts for 60 SMs (k/v_proj at M = 17–48 and qkv_proj at M = 17–32), and o_projand down_proj were back within 0.98–1.01x of stock.

RTX 4090 (128 SMs). Same choices as the first version, so the ~13% stands.

The PR is out of draft now.

A side lesson: noise is bigger than you think

My plan said “no cell more than 3% slower than stock.” On the L4, cells that ran the exact same kernel in both builds still came out anywhere from 0.96x to 1.06x of each other between runs. A single run can’t prove a 3% rule cell by cell.

What made the result trustworthy wasn’t one table. It was that the rule only changes cells that got 18–41% faster, the totals agreed across two separate L4 builds (804.6 and 801.4 µs), and an independent run on different hardware matched the prediction cell for cell.

What I learned

  • Test on the smallest GPU you’re claiming, not the biggest one you have. A change that helps by filling more SMs can backfire on a card with fewer of them.
  • Count waves before tuning tiles. blocks ÷ SMs, rounded up, explained a regression that looked random.
  • Say what you didn’t test. My PR said “only measured on a 4090.” That one line is what made someone with a 4500 Ada run it.
  • Good review is someone else’s hardware. The most useful thing that happened to this PR wasn’t my code. It was a reviewer posting every number.

Links

  • PR: vLLM #62128 (open, ready for review)
  • Issue: vLLM #56924
  • Earlier posts: Blockwise FP8 on Ada GPUs, part 2: my kernel was correct and 4x too slow

My GPU fix was 13% faster on one card and 81% slower on another was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Agentic Core, Deterministic Shell — A pattern for running coding agents you don’t have to watch
partialText:
My coding agent said it read our coding standards. It read 80 lines. A pattern for running coding agents you don’t have to watch.

Three weeks ago I let Claude review a change. The review came back clean, and Claude made a point of telling me it had read our coding standards and checked the change against them. Then I checked the logs: head -80 on the standards file. It read the first 80 lines, and that was "reading the coding standards".

The agent did not lie, at least not on purpose. It decided for itself what “read” means, and 80 lines felt like enough.

The fix took me one field in one place. But it was only that easy because of where I had ended up after about five months of working on dev loops with coding agents. And I think the way there is more interesting than the fix, because a lot of developers are somewhere on that same way right now.

How I got here

Step 1: one big skill

It started with a very big skill, my next-work skill. It was huge. It did the whole loop: pick the next issue, implement it, delegate to the verification, fix what came back. And everything in there was in English. No scripts at all.

It was a bit like a huge shell script. It reminded me very much of the shell scripts we wrote to deploy services: huge, with lots of cases in there for different behaviors, frontend tests here, backend tests there, some conditions. Only that here it was all text.

And yes, mostly it got followed. But it was hard to maintain, and hard to measure what was getting better. Sometimes it ran the UI tests twice, and we couldn’t really figure out why. We corrected the prompt and it was better. Then we wanted to change something in the interaction with beads, our issue tracker, and we had to find all the places where it lived. All these commands were scattered across one big skill.

Of course you can do that with the help of AI too, and get everything consistent again. But why? Why take the risk of not controlling your development flow, if you can spend the same amount of prompts on controlling it?

Step 2: lots of small skills

So the next step was to split the one big skill into lots of sub-skills, called one after the other. Implement, verify, fix, merge: basically the steps of a pipeline, each one a skill of its own. Overall it was easier to manage, but there was still room for improvement.

Step 3: get the scripts out

But the sub-skills still did a lot of small work inline: running a guard, checking the length of the documentation, reading out the beads issue. All of that the agent had to understand and do itself. So we refactored a lot of it out of the skills into little helper scripts. That saved tokens and also sped up the whole skill, because a script just gets executed and doesn’t have to be understood by the agent. The agent only processed the result.

That was good. But the scripts were small helpers within the flow, not the flow itself. Everything was still wrapped in little step skills, and the flow still lived in the prompts.

Step 4: turn it around

I still thought that’s not the best way. Maybe we can turn it around: put the deterministic part outside, around everything, and let the agent only do the work inside one step.

If you have a skill today that calls other skills, you are probably somewhere around step 2 or 3. That’s not a bad place. But it is worth asking which decisions your agent still makes that a few lines of code could make for it.

The pattern

Gary Bernhardt coined “functional core, imperative shell” years ago: keep the logic in a pure core and push everything messy, like I/O, to a thin shell around it. For coding agents I’d turn that around, because there the messy part is in the middle:

Agentic core, deterministic shell.

  • The core is the agent. It does the creative work in one step: implement an issue, review a diff, fix the findings. Inside that step it can be as clever as it wants.
  • The shell is plain code and configuration. It decides what the agent gets as input, checks what comes back, and picks the next step. It never asks the agent what happens next.

If that sounds like CI, that is exactly the idea. Nobody asks a developer “do the tests pass?” and merges on a yes. We let the pipeline run the tests. A coding agent deserves the same treatment, it just never got a pipeline.

With the shell around the agent, three patterns become possible. None of them is new. But you can only use them reliably when code holds control.

Output-driven behavior. Don’t tell the agent what to do, tell it what it has to hand back. Every claim that matters becomes a field. To fill the field, the agent has to do the work. And because the shell knows the input, it can check the output against it. If it doesn’t match, the step fails, the agent gets the log and tries again. That’s the back pressure.

Need-to-know context. The step gets only what it needs, and the shell prepares it. That puts you much more in control of the context. For example, depending on the stack: if the changes are in the frontend, you point the agent to the documentation and coding rules for the frontend. If they’re in the backend, you point it to the backend docs and ADRs, instead of relying on the agent to discover them on its own. And because you prepare the context, you can test it and iterate on it. You can even A/B test it: take the one step, run it with three versions of its input, and compare the outputs side by side. That’s how I found the right inputs, and sometimes even the right outputs.

Lazy agent. Sometimes the best choice is not to run the agent at all. The deterministic shell decides whether an agent needs to run or not. For example, a simple git merge can run through, or it can run into a conflict. A conflict is complicated, so the agent takes over and resolves it. If the merge was clean, we just go on.

Back to the review

The head -80 review happened after step 4. The review was already a step of its own, with the shell around it. The shell routed it correctly: the review passed, so the run went on. But it could only check what the step gave back, and "I read the coding standards" was a sentence in the agent's answer. Still the agent's word.

So the fix was one change in the step’s output. Next to the findings, the agent now has to list the coding standards it applied. That alone did it: to fill the list the agent has to read all of them, there is no way around it with 80 lines. And because the list is data and not a sentence, the shell can check it too. Our standards have 21 rules, so the eval checks that the list has 21 entries. If not, the step failed.

That’s output-driven behavior: the question “did you read it?” is no longer answered by the agent’s word. It is a field you can check.

What step 4 looks like: sous

The shell I built for this is sous (https://sousfactory.com/), and it is open source. You describe your development flow as a graph in YAML, like a GitHub Actions workflow, and sous runs it on your machine with the claude or codex CLI you already have.

Here is a shortened part of the task flow from the starter:

- id: review
  uses: review
  agent: { kind: claude, model: claude-opus-5-5 }
  with:
    diffRange: ${{ steps.implement.commits[0] + "^..HEAD" }}
    criteria:  ${{ ctx.work.body }}
  routes:
    - to: sync
      when: res.ok
    - to: blocked
      when: steps.review.visits >= 3
    - to: fix
      else: true

If the review passes, the run goes on to sync with main; if not, it goes to fix and back, until the third review stops it. None of these decisions is made by the agent.

Each step is a folder in your repository: a Markdown prompt, a JSON Schema for the output and, optionally, two small pieces of TypeScript around it. prepare runs before the agent and decides if the agent runs at all, that’s the lazy agent. eval runs after the agent and judges the work. It can be a function or just npm test. If it fails, the agent gets the log and tries again, up to a cap. After the cap the run stops blocked instead of guessing.

What the shell gives you

Two more things come for free:

  • A second opinion by design. Each step names its own agent and model. Claude can implement and Codex can review, so the reviewer is not the same model checking its own work.
  • Runs you can resume. A blocked run keeps its worktree. You fix the problem by hand, run the same command again, and it continues at that step.

Try it

sous gives you a simple way to design a workflow for your agent. Try it on one issue in your own repository. You need Node 22, gh auth login, and claude or codex on your PATH:

npm install -D sous-factory
npx sous init
cd .sous
./sous validate
./sous run bench <issue>      # smoke test, touches nothing

The code is on GitHub at github.com/sousfactory/sous, MIT licensed, and sousfactory.com has the overview.

If you are somewhere on this way yourself, with one big skill or a chain of small ones, I’d like to hear where you are and what made you move. And if your agent ever told you it read something it didn’t, I’d like to hear that too.

I dictated this article and edited it with AI help. The experience, the opinions and the mistakes are mine.

Agentic Core, Deterministic Shell — A pattern for running coding agents you don’t have to watch was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
